planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in fall into humus-rich, consistently moist soil beneath redwood or Douglas-fir canopy; seed germination is slow and erratic, so nursery stock is propagated almost entirely by division.

directions: This low rhizomatous perennial carries three-lobed, deltoid leaflets and single white, anemone-style flowers held just above the foliage in spring, forming loose colonies along moist redwood-forest stream terraces from northern California into Washington. Plant divisions in fall so roots can settle before the dry season, and mulch with leaf litter to mimic the duff layer it grows in naturally. It spreads steadily but not aggressively, making a good companion for ferns and other shade perennials rather than a thug that crowds them out. Expect full colonies to take two seasons to knit together into a weed-suppressing patch.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Direct-sow seed with the first fall rains into well-drained, duff-covered soil beneath an open redwood or oak-margin canopy; the small basal bulblets it produces can also be lifted and replanted to spread an existing patch.

directions: A delicate forest-floor ephemeral with scalloped basal leaves and a wiry stem of small, deeply cleft pink-white starry flowers that open in late winter and early spring before the overhead canopy fully leafs out. It times its whole life cycle to the rainy season, germinating with fall rains, blooming in the brief light window of early spring, and going dormant underground as a small bulb-like corm through the dry summer. Site it in dry shade at the base of oaks or along redwood-forest margins where light reaches the ground part of the day, and leave the soil undisturbed through dormancy since the corms resent summer digging. It self-sows modestly and naturalizes well alongside other spring ephemerals like shooting stars and checker lily.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall directly where it will grow, in dry, duff-covered shade beneath conifers or oaks; the hooked, velcro-like seed coat that disperses the species in the wild also makes bare-root transplanting of seedlings awkward, so direct seeding or potted starts work best.

directions: One of the few true forget-me-not relatives adapted to dry shade, this herbaceous perennial sends up broad, hound's-tongue-shaped basal leaves in late winter followed by branching stalks of sky-blue, white-throated flowers from February into April. After flowering it sets bristly, hooked seeds and then goes fully dormant for the summer, disappearing completely until the leaves resprout with fall rain. Because it tolerates the deep dry shade under a closed redwood or oak canopy where few flowering natives persist, it is best used as an underplanting beneath established trees rather than in open beds. The species is now also sold under the newer name Adelinia grandis at some native nurseries.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring into moist, humus-rich soil in bright, open shade rather than deep shade; it is a plant of forest margins and streamside groves, not the darkest understory.

directions: Merten's sedge forms upright, gracefully arching clumps of fresh-green blades topped in late spring by distinctive drooping, soft, tassel-like flower spikes unlike the stiffer seedheads of most native sedges. It occurs through moist, open conifer forest and streamside groves from the redwood belt of northern California north into Alaska, favoring the brighter edges of the canopy rather than solid shade. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season, especially the first year after planting, and give it room to form a full-sized clump rather than crowding it against denser groundcovers. It pairs well with ferns and broadleaf woodland wildflowers as a textural, grass-like accent along a shaded path or creek bank.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in early spring into consistently moist, organically rich soil along a shaded stream terrace or seep; give it room, since established colonies spread steadily by rhizome and can cover a large area over several years.

directions: A tall, lush woodland perennial with finely divided, fern-like foliage and arching racemes of tubular pink flowers that open from spring into early summer, found along moist stream terraces and seeps in Douglas-fir and redwood-margin forest from Vancouver Island south into the southern Oregon coast. It wants the dappled light of a streamside opening rather than dense shade, and consistently wet, humus-rich soil to support its vigorous rhizome spread. Because it can colonize a seep or shaded bed quite thoroughly within a few seasons, reserve it for naturalistic plantings with room to roam rather than a tightly curated border. Foliage dies back by late summer as the plant goes dormant, so plan companion ferns or sedges to fill the gap.
